7:14: Amos is using a son of a prophet as a common expression of the culture to mean “a disciple of a prophet.” He is making a point that he did not make his living as a prophet as those who were considered part of the official group of prophets did.
The term sycamore figs describes a kind of fruit that grows on a large tree that was common in the warm, low-lying areas of that region.
7:16: Here, the word of the Lord represents the message that the Lord is speaking through Amos.
Amaziah is speaking of prophesying or preaching as if it were words that drip from the prophet’s mouth, letting words fall like rain.

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Isaac means all the people descended from the patriarch Isaac which is all the people of Israel.
7:17: The implication is that enemy soldiers will capture the city and force Amaziah’s wife to become a prostitute.
Here, the measuring line represents “the parceling out of land to new owners,” since people used such a line to mark off the boundaries of property.
The implication is that unclean ground is a foreign land where people worship other gods, so that it is not a fit place for a worshiper of the Lord to live.
8:2: The word translated as summer fruit sounds very much like the word for end. The Lord’s purpose in showing Amos summer fruit was to give him a prophecy of the end of his people.
8:3: The phrase in that day refers to that time when the Lord will punish them, also referred to as “the day of the Lord” in chapter 5.
8:4: Amos is speaking of these people oppressing needy people as if they were trampling them underfoot.
By cause the afflicted of the land to cease, Amos means that they brought about the ruin of the poor because of their unfair treatment which afflicted them.
8:5: מָתַי יַעֲבֹר הַחֹדֶשׁ וְנַשְׁבִּירָה שֶּׁבֶר וְהַשַּׁבָּת וְנִפְתְּחָה־בָּר
The implication is that the Israelites were not permitted to buy and sell on the festival of the new moon or on the Sabbath, and so these merchants were impatient for those days to end.

The implication is that these merchants would measure out grain in a container smaller than a standard ephah and weigh their customers’ silver with a weight heavier than a standard shekel, so that they cheated the people who bought from them.
8:6: The implication is that a pair of sandals would only cost a very small amount. This means that they were buying needy people as slaves for a price as low as the price of a pair of sandals.
8:7: As in 6:8, the pride of Jacob could refer to: (1) the land of Israel, since that is its meaning elsewhere, and it would make no sense to swear by something negative, such as sinful pride; or (2) the Lord himself. This would then be equivalent to the phrase in 6:8, “The Lord God has sworn by his soul.”
Here, Jacob represents the descendants of Jacob, the people of Israel.

Following the custom of the culture, the Lord is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”), which would be the penalty for not telling the truth. Normally the penalty would be understood to be something general such as “may the Lord punish me severely,” yielding something like, “If I ever forget…, then may the Lord punish me severely…” But since the Lord is speaking, stating this would not make sense.
8:8: הַעַל זֹאת לֹא־תִרְגַּז הָאָרֶץ וְאָבַל כָּל־יוֹשֵׁב בָּהּ
The Lord is using the question form to emphasize that the land will certainly tremble and that everyone living in it will certainly mourn.
וְעָלְתָה כָאֹר כֻּלָּהּ וְנִגְרְשָׁה ונשקה כִּיאוֹר מִצְרָיִם
The point of this comparison is that just as the Nile of Egypt rises in flood and then sinks back down again, so the whole land of Israel will heave up and down.
8:9: The phrase in that day refers to that time when the Lord will punish them.
וְהֵבֵאתִי הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בַּצָּהֳרָיִם וְהַחֲשַׁכְתִּי לָאָרֶץ בְּיוֹם אוֹר

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Another approach would be to combine them and express the emphasis in another way.
8:10: Wearing sackcloth and shaving the head were a symbolic actions by which the Lord’s people would show that they were mourning and grieving.
וְשַׂמְתִּיהָ כְּאֵבֶל יָחִיד וְאַחֲרִיתָהּ כְּיוֹם מָר

The point of these comparisons is that just as the death of an only child brings parents the deepest possible grief, and just as a bitter day brings the greatest sorrow, so the people of Israel will grieve when the Lord punishes them.
8:11: The Lord is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
8:12: The Lord is referring to all of the land by naming the extremes, from sea to sea and from the north and to the sunrise.
8:13: The Lord is using the beautiful virgins and the young men, to represent the strongest and healthiest of the people of Israel.
8:14: Here, the guilt of Samaria represents the sin of idolatry practiced by the people there.
Following the custom of the culture, these people are swearing an oath by naming something that they hold sacred when they say By the life of your god, Dan.
Here, by the life of the way of Beersheba represents the god that people traveled to worship at Beersheba.
The Lord is speaking of these people being destroyed with no hope of recovery as if they would fall down and never rise again.
9:1: A capital is the block of stone at the top of a column or pillar, on which the roof of a building rests.
Here, their end represents all the rest of the people who were not killed by the collapse of the temple.
Here, the sword represents warfare, that is, attack by an enemy army.
לֹא־יָנוּס לָהֶם נָס וְלֹא־יִמָּלֵט לָהֶם פָּלִיט

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional.
9:2: Here, my hand represents the power of the Lord to act.

Here and in the next verse, Amos lists a series of an unreal, hypothetical situations that make the point that no matter where the people would try to hide themselves in order to escape the Lord’s judgment, the Lord will still find and punish them.
9:3: Here, the head represents the top of the mountain called Carmel.
9:4: Here, to the face of represents being in the presence of or in front of those enemies.
Here, the sword represents the enemies who would use swords to kill them.

The Lord is using I will set my eye on them as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will watch them closely,” usually in a positive sense of caring for them but here it is reversed in that it means he is watching them in order to harm them and not to help them.
9:6: The word translated as stairs represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Some scholars have proposed, however, that a scribe may have added an extra letter to this word. Without the extra letter, it would say “upper rooms,” which is how some modern versions translate.
A vault is a kind of arched or domed roof. Amos uses the term to describe the sky as a dome stretched over the earth.
9:7: הֲלוֹא כִבְנֵי כֻשִׁיִּים אַתֶּם לִי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל

The Lord is using the question form to insist that the Israelites are no longer more privileged in his sight than any of these other people groups because they have broken their special covenant with him.

The Lord is speaking as if the people of the nation of Cush, which is modern day Ethiopia, were actually the sons of Cush who was the son of Ham, and the people of Israel where the actual sons of the patriarch, Israel.
The Lord is using the question form to remind the Israelites that he is the one who controls where nations come and go just as he brought Israel out of Egypt.
9:8: Amos is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
Here, the eyes of the Lord God represents his watchful attention.

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Jacob figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel.
9:9: Amos is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
וַהֲנִעוֹתִי בְכָל־הַגּוֹיִם אֶת־בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּאֲשֶׁר יִנּוֹעַ בַּכְּבָרָה

The point of this comparison is that just as grain is shaken in the sieve in order to sort it, so the Lord will shake the house of Israel among all of the nations, which included exile and dispersement among other nations, in order to separate the faithful people from the unfaithful ones.
The Lord is speaking of all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel, as if they were one house.
A sieve is a kind of container with holes in the bottom that a farmer shakes in order to separate grain from stones and dirt.

The meaning of the word translated as pebble could also be translated as “small grain,” and thus it is uncertain whether the grain stays in the sieve or passes through. In either case, the meaning of the comparison is the same; God is using the nations as a sieve to sort out the people of Israel into those who are faithful to him (the grain) and those who are not (the stones). To summarize, this word could mean: (1) a small stone. (2) a small piece of something, such as grain. In this case, the sieve is retaining the grain and letting the small stones fall through.
9:10: The sinners are speaking of suffering harm as if The evil were a living thing that could approach or reach them.
9:11: The Lord is speaking as if the dynasty or kingdom of David were a booth, a temporary shelter, that had collapsed and that he would restore or raise up again. He goes on to speak of repairing its breaches and rebuilding its ruins.
9:13: The Lord is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say about the days or the specific time that is coming.
וְנִגַּשׁ חוֹרֵשׁ בַּקֹּצֵר וְדֹרֵךְ עֲנָבִים בְּמֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע

The implication is that the harvests will be so large that the plowing and planting seasons will begin before the reaping and the treading of grapes are finished. This was one of the covenant promises mentioned in Leviticus 26:5.
The Lord is speaking as if the mountains and the hills themselves were producing sweet wine in such quantity that it flowed down their slopes.
9:14: The Lord is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
9:15: וּנְטַעְתִּים עַל־אַדְמָתָם וְלֹא יִנָּתְשׁוּ עוֹד מֵעַל אַדְמָתָם
The Lord is speaking of restoring the Israelites to their land as if they were plants that he would plant in the ground that would never be uprooted again.
